Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 104, verses 1–3:

(p-6253) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Humazah

Meccan, and its verses are nine.

(p-6254) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1–3] ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker,﴾ ﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it,﴾ ﴿thinking that his wealth will make him immortal.﴾

﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker﴾, i.e., woe to everyone who defames people's honour and backbites them. Its root is from al-hamz (crushing, breaking) and al-lamz (striking with the tongue, reviling), in their literal senses; then it was used metaphorically for this, and then it became a conventional literal meaning for it. Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"You show affection when you meet me, lying, but when I am absent you are the one who mocks and reviles."

The pattern fu'alah indicates that this is a habit of his which he has become accustomed to, since it is among the forms of intensification. The verse is meant to refer to those among the polytheists in Mecca who were hammazun lammazun (constant mockers and slanderers), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29] ﴿And when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 30], and His saying: ﴿a slanderer, going about with malicious gossip﴾ [al-Qalam: 11], and the verses thereafter. Although the cause is specific, the threat is general, encompassing everyone who engages in that vile conduct. The secret of its being stated in general terms is that it serves as an allusive rebuke to the one concerned, for that is more effective in deterring him and more painful to him.

﴿who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾ [al-Humazah: 2], i.e., he counted its number and did not spend it in the paths of righteousness.

The Imam said: That which drives him to belittle people's worth is his gathering of wealth and counting it, i.e., counting it again and again, out of his infatuation with it and his delight in tallying it, for he sees no honour, nobility, or glory apart from it. (p-6255) Whenever he looks at the abundance he has of it, he becomes puffed up and thinks that it places him at such a high rank that every person of merit and distinction is beneath him. So he mocks them, scorns them, and defames them, and then he does not fear that punishment may befall him for the scorning, defaming, and tearing of honour, because his delusion with wealth has made him forget death and diverted him from remembering the outcome. Thus, ﴿thinking that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ [al-Humazah: 3], i.e., he supposes that his wealth, which he gathered, counted, and was stingy in spending, will make him eternal in this world, thereby removing death from him.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:**

[4–9] ﴿No! He will surely be thrown into the Crushing Fire.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing Fire is?﴾ [al-Humazah: 5] ﴿It is the fire of God, kindled,﴾ [al-Humazah: 6] ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ [al-Humazah: 7] ﴿Indeed, it is closed over them,﴾ [al-Humazah: 8] ﴿in extended columns.﴾ [al-Humazah: 9]

﴿No!﴾ That is: let him desist from this assumption, for the matter is not as he supposed. Rather, he must depart from this life to another life, in which he will be punished for the evil deeds he earned, as He said: ﴿He will surely be thrown into the Crushing Fire.﴾ That is: he will surely be cast and hurled, on the Day of Resurrection, into the Fire, whose nature is to crush everything cast into it, that is, to break it. The word (*al-nabdh*, "throwing") conveys contempt and belittlement.

﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing Fire is?﴾ [al-Humazah: 5] This is a question about it, to magnify its matter, as if it were not among the things that the intellects can grasp.

﴿It is the fire of God, kindled﴾ [al-Humazah: 6] That is: it is the Fire that is attributed to none but Him, glory be to Him, because He is the one who brings it into being in a world that no one else knows.

Abu al-Su'ud said: In its being attributed to Him, glory be to Him, and in describing it as kindled, there is a magnification of its matter beyond which there is no greater.

﴿which rises over the hearts﴾ [al-Humazah: 7] Ibn Jarir said: That is, the pain of it and its blaze rise over the hearts. (p-٦٢٥٦) *Al-ittila'* (rising over) and *al-bulugh* (reaching) may have the same meaning; it is related from the Arabs by transmission: (*mata tala'ta ardana*, "when did you reach our land?") and (*tala'tu ardi*, "I reached my land"), meaning "I arrived."

Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that it enters their bodies until it reaches their chests and rises over their hearts, which are the centres of the heart. Nothing in the human body is more delicate than the heart (*fu'ad*), and nothing suffers more pain from the slightest harm touching it. So how much more when the Fire of Hell rises over it and takes control of it! It is also permissible that He singles out the hearts because they are the seat of disbelief, corrupt beliefs, and wicked intentions; or it may mean, by way of metaphor, that it looks over the sources that necessitate it.

﴿Indeed, it is closed over them﴾ [al-Humazah: 8] That is: shut and sealed, with no escape for them from it.

﴿in extended columns﴾ [al-Humazah: 9] This is a description of *mu'sadah* (closed), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in the genitive (*al-damir al-majrur*). Al-Zamakhshari alluded to both possibilities with his words: The meaning is that it reinforces their despair of coming out and their certainty of eternal imprisonment, so the doors are closed upon them and they are stretched upon the columns, a binding upon a binding. It is also possible that the meaning is: they are shut upon them, while they are bound in extended columns, like the stocks (*al-maqatir*) in which thieves are placed.

*Al-maqatir* is the plural of *maqtara*, with a fatha, which is a large trunk with holes in which the feet of imprisoned thieves and the like are placed. (*Taqtur*) means that each one is placed beside another. And *'amad* has been read with a damma on the 'ayn and the mim, and with a fatha on both.

Ibn Jarir said: These are two well-known readings (*qira'atan*), each of which was read by scholars of the reciters, and both are sound dialects. The Arabs pluralise *'amud* as *'umud* and *'amad*, with both letters damma or fatha, just as they pluralise *ihab* as *uhub* and *ahab*.

**Note:**

Al-Qashani said, in explaining the afflictions of the two vices of *al-hamz* (defamation) and *al-lamz* (slander), whose punishment the surah addresses, the following, and this is its example: *Al-hamz*, that is, breaking people's honour, and *al-lamz*, that is, attacking them, are two vices composed of ignorance, anger, and arrogance, because they involve harm and seeking to rise above people. The sum is that ignorance, which is the vice of the angelic faculty, is the root of all vices and entails them. Therefore its possessor, immersed in it, deservedly merits the everlasting punishment that overpowers the heart, nullifying its essence.
